papers.title: Beyond a Single Sentiment Score: Topical and Affective Dimensions of Emoji Meaning on Twitter
papers.abstract: Emoji are widely treated as compact affective tokens whose meaning is summarised by a single sentiment score. We argue that this picture is incomplete. From a corpus of 16{,}575 English tweets and a per-emoji metric we call \emph{stability delta} (within-class minus between-class cosine similarity of sentence embeddings), we show that emojis used in tightly clustered topical contexts also exhibit \emph{more} polarised crowd-sourced sentiment, not less. Validated against the Kralj Novak et al.\ (2015) sentiment lexicon, the central correlation is Spearman $\rho = +0.361$ (Holm $p = 0.015$, 95\% bootstrap CI $[+0.10, +0.59]$); against the independent Ferr\'{e} et al.\ (2025) Spanish 13-emotion ratings, $\rho = +0.509$ ($p = 0.0003$). The result survives permutation testing, BCa bootstrap, leave-one-out jackknife, partial correlation controlling for emoji frequency, and Holm correction across a four-test family. Topical coherence and affective dispersion are distinct dimensions of emoji meaning. As a downstream check we report leakage-free five-fold cross-validation results for sarcasm classification on the Emoji Sarcasm Dataset; all three baselines (a gated multimodal architecture, fine-tuned BERTweet features, and fine-tuned RoBERTa features) score above 0.97 macro F1, indicating the dataset has saturating emoji-label cues. We frame the classifier as supporting evidence rather than the contribution.

papers.title: Do LLMs Really Lack Difference Awareness? Uncovering Heuristic Substitution in Group-Differentiating Fairness
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the issue of difference awareness in LLMs, defined as a model's ability to recognize and acknowledge meaningful differences between social groups in fairness decision-making. Previous studies have consistently shown that models perform poorly on such tasks, a finding commonly attributed to a lack of difference awareness. We propose an alternative account, which we term Fairness Heuristic Substitution: difference awareness is not necessarily absent, but the complex demand of simultaneously identifying relevant group differences and determining their implications for fairness decisions may lead models to substitute the simpler, more accessible equal-treatment heuristic, i.e., formal equality. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce TDD, a Two-stage Distinguish-Decide framework that explicitly decomposes fairness reasoning into first distinguishing contextually relevant group differences and then making the corresponding decision, thereby discouraging reliance on formal-equality shortcuts. (i) Across four benchmarks and ten models ranging from billions to trillions of parameters, TDD significantly outperforms one-stage baselines, even one strengthened through simulated test-set leakage. (ii) Combining TDD with neuron-level contrastive probing provides mechanistic evidence consistent with the Fairness Heuristic Substitution hypothesis by revealing two signatures of the formal-equality: a compact, locally coordinated representational structure and a pronounced activation bias under default reasoning. (iii) TDD's stage-wise decomposition uncovers overlooked failure modes in fairness reasoning, including heuristic displacement and misaligned stage dynamics.

papers.title: Large Teams Consistently Develop Science
papers.abstract: Scientific progress depends on both developing established knowledge and disrupting it to make way for new ideas. Using the disruption index (D), our previous work showed that large teams tend to develop science, while small teams are more likely to disrupt it. Recent work challenges this finding, arguing that D mechanically depends on reference-list length. Using an alternative measure (oneD), it reaches the opposite conclusion: large teams are more disruptive. Combining Nobel Prize case studies, mathematical analysis, and large-scale publication data, we show that oneD misclassifies developmental contributions as disruptive and introduces the very sensitivity to reference-list length that it seeks to eliminate. The original measure, D, however, shows no evidence of the claimed systematic dependence on reference-list length. More fundamentally, even after controlling for reference-list length, larger teams remain more likely to produce strongly developmental work. Our findings reaffirm that large teams consistently develop science and offer new insights into the measurement of scientific disruption.

papers.title: A mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
papers.abstract: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent that finds a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade, the model built for rumour and adoption spread on social networks, now embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd, so the swarm aggregates on a resource and then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and space are one coupled system, and this feedback, not any tuning, makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than reaching near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a question of percolation. The swarm holds itself in a cascade window that is locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, self-limiting drive-release cycle, sandpile-like but non-conservative. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours that foraging biology documents separately emerge together: recruitment to discoveries, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These follow from one least-committal principle, the resource field and the search both as maximum entropy, with Levy search matched to the field's sparsity and recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging appear as one system seen in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. That sparse, clustered field is also the generic one, because resources almost inevitably aggregate, so one untuned rule should recur widely.

papers.title: DeGroot Dynamics on Multiplex Networks with Directed and Acyclic Interlayer Connectivities
papers.abstract: In models of opinion dynamics, researchers typically examine how an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced by the opinions of their neighbors in a network. However, people's opinions on a topic are also influenced by their opinions and their neighbors' opinions on related topics. In an election, for example, the opinions of a voter on a variety of issues inform their opinions of electoral candidates. To consider the influence between people's opinions on multiple distinct topics, we study a multiplex extension of the traditional DeGroot consensus model. In our multiplex DeGroot model, different network layers represent distinct topics and directed interlayer edges (which are not allowed to form cycles) encode relationships between distinct topics. In our model, an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced both by the opinions of their neighbors on that topic and by their own opinions on related topics. We prove under mild conditions that our multiplex DeGroot model converges to a limit state. We also prove that strong connectedness in ``source layers'' (which represent fundamental beliefs) eventually yields a consensus opinion in each layer. In particular, we show that consensus on source layers can lead to consensus on other layers even when those layers otherwise would be polarized. By numerically simulating our multiplex DeGroot model on a two-layer network, we examine the effects on opinion dynamics of (1) different network structures and (2) different types of initial opinion data.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Model for the Evolution of a Social Network
papers.abstract: Echo chambers and filter bubbles provide a framework to view communication and connection in a social network age. Such systems are characterised by isolated communities regurgitating information which reinforces prior beliefs. Theoretical analysis of echo chambers is suited for a network science approach to understand the mechanics of information influences between users. Here, we propose an evolutionary network model that extends the Quoter Model, rewiring edges according to cross-entropy between text-generating nodes. Parameters characterise binary reinforcement vs exploration node intents, determining whether a node will seek high or low novelty neighbours, measured by cross-entropy. Through an empirical simulation study, we observe emergent model attributes. Specifically, we compare to a Watts--Strogatz model, highlighting parameter regions of high clustering and hyper-exploration. Further, we identify a quality of disjoint communities akin to rudimentary echo chamber structures. These findings underscore user behaviours that drive echo chamber entrenchment, contextualising future social network analysis.

papers.title: A Geometric Principle for Path Selection in Directed Acyclic Graphs
papers.abstract: There are many types of path between nodes of a Directed acyclic graph (DAG), including the shortest and longest paths. Here, we ask whether the choice of path used in any analysis reflects the geometry of the latent space in which the DAG is embedded. To do this we define L_p-cube spacetimes, a family of continuous ordered spaces in which a single parameter p determines whether the ordered distance satisfies the ordered triangle identity when p>1, or the reverse ordered triangle identity when 0<p<1 or p<0, both of which are rarely studied. The forward connection kernel in the p<0 case has infinite hyper-volume, yet it is a well defined model. We then construct random geometric DAGs embedded in our L_p-cube spacetime and study their geometry. For p>1, where the ordered triangle identity holds, the shortest paths provide the closest approximation to the continuum ordered geodesic while for 0<p<1 and p<0, where the reverse ordered triangle identity holds, this role is instead taken by the longest weighted path. We also test the robustness of this relationship in a geometric citation model in which the random geometric DAG is supplemented by a preferential-attachment-type mechanism allowing connections beyond the strict geometric cut-off. The same broad correspondence between latent geometry and ordered geodesic path type is recovered. Our results show that the preference for shortest or longest paths in a DAG is closely connected to the geometry assumed for its latent space, and suggest that path structure can provide information about latent geometry, even when that geometry is not directly observed.

papers.title: Percolation in the Stochastic Block Model
papers.abstract: The stochastic block model is a paradigmatic model of networks with community structure. Yet percolation in the model has been studied primarily in cases with a fixed block structure, even though in real networks, the community structure may evolve as the network grows. Here we study percolation in sequences of stochastic block models in which the numbers and sizes of communities, as well as the intra- and intercommunity connection probabilities may all change with the network size. We analyze five such sequences using two methods: linearized self-consistent equations for the locally tree-like models and a branching process at the community scale for the models with nonvanishing clustering. We find that the critical average degree is not generally equal to $1$, even in locally tree-like sequences, because the transition depends on how connections are distributed across the evolving community structure. We also show that the community-scale branching process accurately predicts the transition when intercommunity connections are sufficiently sparse, even in the presence of nonvanishing clustering, while a geometric stochastic block model sequence demonstrates the limitations of this method when correlations between intercommunity connections cannot be neglected. These results extend percolation studies in the stochastic block model to more realistic scenarios with evolving community structure, and may provide new methods to derive the upper and lower bounds for the percolation threshold in geometric long-range percolation.

papers.title: From Debate to Decision: Conformal Social Choice for Safe Multi-Agent Deliberation
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate improves LLM reasoning, yet agreement is not evidence of correctness. When agents converge on a wrong answer through social reinforcement, consensus stopping commits that error to automated action with no recourse. We introduce Conformal Social Choice, a post-hoc layer that converts debate outputs into calibrated act-versus-escalate decisions. Verbalized probability distributions from heterogeneous agents are aggregated via a linear opinion pool and calibrated with split conformal prediction, yielding fixed-round marginal coverage: at any pre-specified round, the correct answer is included with probability ${\geq}\,1{-}\alpha$, without assumptions on individual model calibration. A hierarchical action policy maps singletons to autonomous action and larger sets to human escalation. Across eight MMLU-Pro domains and two additional benchmarks, fixed-round coverage stays close to target. The key finding is not that debate becomes more accurate, but that the conformal layer makes its failures actionable: at the final round, 81.9\% of wrong-consensus cases are flagged by non-singleton sets at $\alpha{=}0.05$. Separately, among cases that reach a singleton before the final round, accuracy reaches 90.0--96.8\% on MMLU-Pro (up to 22.1pp above consensus stopping): a selection effect, not a reasoning improvement. Simple probability- and entropy-threshold rules attain comparable interception; conformal's distinct value is a finite-sample fixed-round coverage guarantee together with explicit candidate sets for escalation. Adaptive first-singleton stopping is evaluated empirically and not covered by this guarantee.

papers.title: Matching Markets: Equilibrium Computation, Indivisible Goods, and Positional Externalities
papers.abstract: Matching markets provide a mathematical framework for allocating scarce resources among strategic agents with heterogeneous preferences. While matching without money relies on ordinal stability and Pareto efficiency, Fisher and Arrow--Debreu markets mediate allocation through budgets and market-clearing prices. In this paper, we study the convex-analytic foundations, computational complexity, and external-utility extensions of Fisher matching markets. First, we formulate fractional resource allocation and linear Fisher markets via Fenchel conjugate duality and the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Eisenberg--Gale convex program, showing how budget-weighted Nash social welfare characterizes competitive equilibria across linear and homothetic utility families. Second, we review topological existence via Sperner's lemma alongside polynomial-time combinatorial algorithms for divisible markets, including the Devanur--Papadimitriou--Saberi--Vazirani (DPSV) primal-dual max-flow algorithm and Orlin's strongly polynomial scaling algorithm. Third, we contrast the tractability of divisible markets with the $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness and $\mathsf{PPAD}$-completeness of indivisible Fisher markets and Competitive Equilibrium from Equal Incomes (CEEI), comparing $\varepsilon$-approximate equilibria, CEEI-FRAC, and Budish's Approximate CEEI mechanism. Finally, we analyze Fisher markets with positional (snob-effect) externalities, where buyer $i$'s utility for good $j$ scales with her relative share $(x_{ij}/\sum_{k} x_{kj})^{\alpha_i}$ for $\alpha_i > 0$. We prove that positional utility summands are convex on the nonnegative orthant, so utilitarian social welfare is maximized at exclusive corner allocations, whereas decentralized price-taking admits a unique budget-proportional equilibrium in single-good snob markets with a Price of Anarchy of $n^\alpha$ among $n$ symmetric buyers.

papers.title: Inference of Hierarchical Core-Periphery Structure in Temporal Networks
papers.abstract: Networks can have various types of mesoscale structures. One such structure is core--periphery structure, which consists of sets of densely-connected core nodes and sets of sparsely-connected peripheral nodes. Core nodes are connected densely to other core nodes and are potentially connected densely to peripheral nodes, which are connected sparsely to other nodes. There has been much research on core--periphery structure in time-independent networks, but few core--periphery detection methods have been developed for time-dependent (i.e., ``temporal") networks. Using a multilayer-network representation of temporal networks and an inference approach that employs stochastic block models, we generalize a recent method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure \cite{Polanco23} from time-independent networks to temporal networks. In contrast to ``onion-like'' nested core--periphery structures (where each node is assigned to a group according to how deeply it is nested in a network's core), hierarchical core--periphery structures encompass networks with nested structures, tree-like structures (where any two groups must either be disjoint or have one group as a strict subset of the other group), and general non-nested mesoscale structures (where the group assignments of nodes do not have to be nested in any way). To perform statistical inference and thereby identify hierarchical core--periphery structure, we use a Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. We illustrate our method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure in one synthetic temporal network and two real-world temporal networks, and we discuss the structures that we identify in these networks.

papers.title: Higher-Order Network Structure Inference: A Topological Approach to Network Selection
papers.abstract: Thresholding---the pruning of nodes or edges based on their properties or weights---is an essential preprocessing tool for extracting interpretable structure from complex network data, yet existing methods face several key limitations. Threshold selection often relies on heuristic methods or trial and error due to large parameter spaces and unclear optimization criteria, leading to sensitivity where small parameter variations produce significant changes in network structure. Moreover, most approaches focus on pairwise relationships between nodes, overlooking critical higher-order interactions involving three or more nodes. We introduce a systematic thresholding algorithm that uses topological data analysis to identify optimal network parameters by accounting for higher-order structural relationships. Our method uses persistent homology to favor thresholds at which the network's topological representation is stable under small parameter changes, subject to minimum requirements for higher-order features. Hyperparameters allow users to specify minimum requirements for topological features, effectively constraining the parameter search to avoid spurious solutions. We demonstrate the approach using networks of concepts linked by co-occurrence in scientific abstracts. Across scientific fields, paired comparisons with ten alternative thresholds favor our method at the median for finite-feature density and normalized total persistence in homological dimensions one and two. Our approach allows researchers to incorporate domain-specific constraints and extends beyond network thresholding to general parameterization problems in data analysis.

papers.title: Borda Aggregation Dynamics of Preference Orderings on Networks
papers.abstract: We introduce and analyze a discrete-time network process in which each node holds a (weak) preference ordering over a finite set of alternatives and updates by local Borda aggregation. At each step, a node forms a weighted average (row-stochastic random-walk normalization) of its neighbors' Borda score vectors and projects the aggregated score back to a weak order. Updates are bounded: in each round, a node advances by at most one step along a shortest path in the fixed graph of preference orderings, following the direction prescribed by its neighbors' Borda-aggregated preferences. Our emphasis is dynamical: we develop sufficient conditions, stated directly in terms of graph topology, weights, and the bounded step rule, for (i) self-sustained oscillations in the absence of persistent sources, and (ii) forced oscillations under contrarian persistent camps. We also record robustness (structural stability) away from score-tie hyperplanes and contrast synchronous (Variant S) and asynchronous (Variant A) updating.
